section.title: The Northern Campaign
section.sectionRationale: The conquest sweeps north. A vast coalition under Jabin of Hazor gathers with horses and chariots, an army like the sand of the seashore, but God tells Joshua not to fear and delivers them. Joshua takes Hazor and the northern cities, even the feared Anakim, and at last the whole land is taken and the land has rest from war. It is one movement, the northern campaign, which completes the conquest and shows God faithful to give the whole land, exactly as He promised Moses.
section.thesis: Against the largest, best-armed enemy yet, God again wins the victory and hands over the land, so that Joshua leaves nothing undone of all the LORD commanded Moses; even the dreaded giants fall, and the God who promised the land proves faithful to give it, granting His people rest from war.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the northern coalition gathers and God promises victory, verses 1 to 9; the fall of Hazor and the northern cities, verses 10 to 15; the whole land taken, including the Anakim, verses 16 to 22; and the land at rest, verse 23.

units.label: The northern coalition and God's promise
units.note: do not be afraid; by this time tomorrow I will deliver them

verses.text: Now when Jabin king of Hazor heard about these things, he sent word to Jobab king of Madon; to the kings of Shimron and Achshaph;
to the kings of the north in the mountains, in the Arabah south of Chinnereth, in the foothills, and in Naphoth-dor to the west;
to the Canaanites in the east and west; to the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, and Jebusites in the hill country; and to the Hivites at the foot of Hermon in the land of Mizpah.
So these kings came out with all their armies, a multitude as numerous as the sand on the seashore, along with a great number of horses and chariots.
All these kings joined forces and encamped at the waters of Merom to fight against Israel.
Then the LORD said to Joshua, “Do not be afraid of them, for by this time tomorrow I will deliver all of them slain before Israel. You are to hamstring their horses and burn up their chariots.”
So by the waters of Merom, Joshua and his whole army came upon them suddenly and attacked them,

and the LORD delivered them into the hand of Israel, who struck them down and pursued them all the way to Greater Sidon and Misrephoth-maim, and eastward as far as the Valley of Mizpeh. They struck them down, leaving no survivors.
Joshua treated them as the LORD had told him; he hamstrung their horses and burned up their chariots.

units.label: The fall of Hazor and the northern cities
units.note: leaving nothing undone of all the LORD commanded Moses

verses.text: At that time Joshua turned back and captured Hazor and put its king to the sword, because Hazor was formerly the head of all these kingdoms.
The Israelites put everyone in Hazor to the sword, devoting them to {{cherem|destruction}}. Nothing that breathed remained, and Joshua burned down Hazor itself.
Joshua captured all these kings and their cities and put them to the sword. He devoted them to destruction, as Moses the LORD’s servant had commanded.
Yet Israel did not burn any of the cities built on their mounds, except Hazor, which Joshua burned.
The Israelites took for themselves all the plunder and livestock of these cities, but they put all the people to the sword until they had completely destroyed them, not sparing anyone who breathed.
As the LORD had commanded His servant Moses, so Moses commanded Joshua. That is what Joshua did, leaving nothing undone of all that the LORD had commanded Moses.

units.label: The whole land taken, including the Anakim
units.note: it was of the LORD to harden their hearts

verses.text: So Joshua took this entire region: the hill country, all the Negev, all the land of Goshen, the western foothills, the Arabah, and the mountains of Israel and their foothills,
from Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir, as far as Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon at the foot of Mount Hermon. He captured all their kings and struck them down, putting them to death.
Joshua waged war against all these kings for a long period of time.
No city made peace with the Israelites except the Hivites living in Gibeon; all others were taken in battle.

For it was of the LORD to {{chazaq|harden}} their hearts to engage Israel in battle, so that they would be set apart for destruction and would receive no mercy, being annihilated as the LORD had commanded Moses.

At that time Joshua proceeded to eliminate the Anakim from the hill country of Hebron, Debir, and Anab, and from all the hill country of Judah and of Israel. Joshua devoted them to destruction, along with their cities.
No Anakim were left in the land of the Israelites; only in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod did any survive.

units.label: The land at rest
units.note: then the land had rest from war

verses.text: So Joshua took the entire land, in keeping with all that the LORD had spoken to Moses. And Joshua gave it as an inheritance to Israel according to the allotments to their tribes. Then the land had {{shaqat|rest}} from war.

cherem.gloss: That which is devoted irrevocably to the LORD, here by destruction. As in the south, the northern cities are placed under the cherem, carried out just as Moses the LORD's servant had commanded. The repeated ban frames the conquest as God's judgment under His authority, and the note that Israel kept the plunder while devoting the people shows the ban fell on Canaan's guilty inhabitants, not on greed for spoil.

chazaq.gloss: To be strong, firm; here in the causative sense, to harden or strengthen. The narrator says it was of the LORD to chazaq the hearts of the kings to fight Israel, echoing the hardening of Pharaoh, Exodus 9:12. God's sovereignty stands behind even the enemies' resolve to fight, bringing His righteous judgment on nations already ripe for it, while their own hostility remains truly their own.

shaqat.gloss: To be quiet, at rest, undisturbed. The chapter closes with the land shaqat, at rest from war, the goal toward which the conquest moved. This rest, secured by God's faithfulness to His promise, is a foretaste of the deeper rest to which Joshua's rest points, the Sabbath rest that remains for the people of God in Christ, Hebrews 4:9.

basic.context: The conquest now turns north. Jabin, king of the powerful city of Hazor, rallies a huge coalition of northern kings with horses and chariots, an army as numerous as the sand of the seashore, far bigger than anything Israel has faced. But God tells Joshua the same thing He has said all along: Do not be afraid, for by this time tomorrow I will deliver them. God gives the victory, Joshua hamstrings the horses and burns the chariots so Israel will not trust in them, and Hazor is taken and burned. City by city the north falls. Even the Anakim, the giants who terrified Israel a generation earlier, are driven out. At last the whole land is taken, given to the tribes as their inheritance, and the land has rest from war. The question underneath is: will God keep His promise to give the whole land?
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative, summarizing the completion of the conquest. Its refrain is that Joshua did all that the LORD commanded Moses, tying the whole campaign to God's faithfulness to His word. The hard note that God hardened the kings' hearts must be read alongside the wider biblical teaching on God's sovereignty and human responsibility, and the herem, as before, as His righteous judgment on Canaan. The rest at the end points beyond itself to a greater rest.
basic.originalLanguages: The northern cities are placed under the cherem, devoted to destruction as Moses commanded. God chazaq, hardens, the kings' hearts to fight, bringing His judgment. And the land at last has shaqat, rest, from war, a foretaste of the greater rest.
basic.typology: The defeat of the giants who once terrified Israel, and the securing of rest in the land, point to Christ, who overcomes the powers that terrify His people and brings them into a rest that cannot be lost. The hamstrung horses and burned chariots picture trust in God rather than in worldly might.
basic.christ: The Anakim, the giants whose report once made Israel's heart melt, are finally destroyed, showing that no enemy is too great for the God who fights for His people. So Christ defeats the powers that hold His people in fear, and He brings them into the rest the land only foreshadowed, the Sabbath rest that remains for the people of God, Hebrews 4.
basic.god: God is faithful to His promise, giving the whole land just as He spoke to Moses. He is sovereign over the hearts of kings and the outcome of battles. He is the warrior who delivers a small people from a vast, well-armed enemy. And He is the giver of rest, bringing His people into the settled inheritance He swore to their fathers.
basic.crossReferences: Numbers 13 records the giants who once terrified Israel, now destroyed. Psalm 20 says some trust in chariots, but we trust in the LORD. Deuteronomy 7 promised God would clear the nations before Israel. And Hebrews 4 shows the land's rest as a shadow of the rest in Christ.
basic.oneStory: The conquest is completed as God gives the north, destroys the feared giants, and grants the land rest from war, keeping every promise He made to Moses. It is the fulfillment of the pledge to Abraham, and the rest secured points forward to the greater and lasting rest won by Christ.

context.literary:
Chapter 11 is built to answer chapter 10 rather than merely repeat it. The southern coalition of five kings, verse 5 of chapter 10, is here dwarfed by a northern one that spans an entire region, verses 1 to 3 listing kings and peoples in every direction, north, east, west, hill country and lowland, until the summary line lands with deliberate weight, a multitude as numerous as the sand on the seashore, along with a great number of horses and chariots, verse 4. By escalating the size of the threat, the narrator sets up his real point: the LORD's reassurance to Joshua is word for word what it has been all along, do not be afraid, verse 6, unchanged by the larger scale of the enemy, because the outcome was never a function of the enemy's size in the first place.

The chapter's structure then compresses time rather than events. Verses 10 to 15 narrate what verse 18 admits took a long period of time in six brisk verses, dominated by a formula repeated four times, as Moses the LORD's servant had commanded, verses 12, 15, 20, 23, which functions as the section's real subject; obedience to a decades-old command matters more to the narrator than the mechanics of any single siege. The single most theologically loaded sentence in the chapter, it was of the LORD to harden their hearts, verse 20, sits almost buried inside a summary of conquered territory, forcing the reader to notice that even the enemy's stubborn resistance served a purpose beyond itself. The book's entire conquest narrative then closes on a single, quiet clause, then the land had rest from war, verse 23, four words that carry the weight of everything since chapter 1.
context.historical:
Excavations at Tel Hazor, roughly ten miles north of the Sea of Galilee, have uncovered a Late Bronze Age city of genuinely exceptional size for the region, consistent with the narrator's own description of it as formerly the head of all these kingdoms, verse 10, a phrase suggesting Hazor functioned as something like a regional hegemon over the smaller city-states allied with it. Its destruction layer, marked by intense burning, corresponds to the unique detail that Joshua burned down Hazor itself, verse 11, while explicitly sparing the other captured cities their mounds, verse 13, a restraint that let Israel inhabit existing settlements rather than rebuild from ash everywhere it conquered.

Horses and chariots gave the northern alliance a real tactical advantage that Israel, arriving on foot from the wilderness, simply did not possess, which is presumably why God specifies exactly how Joshua is to neutralize rather than adopt them, hamstring their horses and burn up their chariots, verse 6. Cutting a horse's leg tendons destroyed its usefulness for war without requiring Israel to build or maintain its own chariot corps, keeping the nation dependent on God's power rather than borrowed Canaanite technology, a policy Deuteronomy later makes explicit for any future king, he must not acquire many horses for himself, Deuteronomy 17:16.

The Anakim were remembered as people of unusual stature whose report, decades earlier, had reduced the spies to despair, we seemed like grasshoppers in our own sight, Numbers 13:33, and their defeat here in the hill country of Hebron and Debir directly reverses that earlier failure of nerve. That a remnant survived specifically in the Philistine coastal cities of Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod, verse 22, is no incidental detail; it plants the seed for the Philistine giants Israel would face generations later, most famously Goliath of Gath, 1 Samuel 17:4.
context.canonical:
The chapter closes the conquest narrative that Deuteronomy anticipated and Joshua then fulfills clause by clause; the book itself later reflects on this exact moment with a threefold summary, the LORD gave Israel all the land He had sworn to give their fathers, and the LORD gave them rest on every side, not one of all the LORD's good promises to the house of Israel had failed, everything was fulfilled, Joshua 21:43-45, a passage that functions almost as the theological headline for the events narrated here.

God's hardening of the northern kings' hearts stands inside a pattern that runs from Pharaoh onward, the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he would not listen to them, Exodus 9:12, a sovereignty over human resistance Paul later generalizes, God has mercy on whom He wants to have mercy, and He hardens whom He wants to harden, Romans 9:18, always in service of a judgment the hardened party had already, by its own persistent hostility, earned.

The defeat of the Anakim answers directly to the spies' unbelief a generation earlier, Numbers 13:28-33, and Caleb's own later request for Hebron specifically names them, you yourself heard then that the Anakim were there, with great and fortified cities, perhaps with the LORD's help I will drive them out, Joshua 14:12, so that this chapter's victory becomes the ground on which an old man's long-deferred faith is finally rewarded. And the rest that closes the chapter becomes, centuries later, the very rest the writer of Hebrews says was never final, for if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day, there remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God, Hebrews 4:8-9.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The writer wants the size of the northern threat on the record precisely so that Israel's response to it, hamstringing captured horses rather than claiming them, burning captured chariots rather than fielding them, reads as a deliberate refusal to let victory be explained by anything other than the LORD who had promised it. Facing the largest, best-equipped coalition yet, Joshua is given the identical reassurance offered before every previous battle, do not be afraid, so that the reader understands the outcome was never actually in doubt at any point across the whole conquest, regardless of how the enemy's numbers happened to compare from one chapter to the next. The fourfold repetition of as the LORD commanded Moses tells the reader what mattered most to the author's own generation, that Joshua's obedience was total and unembellished, leaving nothing undone, verse 15, a detail meant to reassure Israel that the land it now occupied was possessed on the exact terms God had specified rather than on terms the nation had negotiated or improved upon for itself.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The chapter describes the God-commanded completion of one particular, non-repeatable conquest, including its total destruction of specific Canaanite cities and its statement that God hardened specific kings' hearts toward a specific judgment; none of this authorizes later peoples to treat military conquest as divinely sanctioned or to explain their own opponents' resistance as divine hardening. What does carry forward is the pattern beneath the specifics. Believers still face the temptation to trust visible, worldly resources, financial security, alliances, technology, over reliance on God, and the same lesson taught by hamstrung horses and burned chariots applies without needing the original command repeated, some trust in chariots and horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God, Psalm 20:7. Likewise the completed obedience Joshua models, leaving nothing undone of all that the LORD had commanded, remains a standing call to wholehearted rather than partial faithfulness, whatever the specific commands a later believer is actually given.

debates.question: What does it mean that the LORD hardened the hearts of the northern kings so they would fight and be destroyed?

views.label: Sovereign confirmation of a hostility already chosen
views.case: As with Pharaoh, whose own heart is said to harden itself before God is ever said to harden it, Exodus 8:15 and 9:12, the pattern in Scripture is that God confirms and gives over a resistance the person or nation had already settled into; the kings' war council in verses 1 to 5 is entirely their own initiative before verse 20 ever mentions hardening, so the hardening ratifies a choice already made rather than manufacturing one that would not otherwise exist.

views.label: A judicial handing-over serving a judgment centuries in the making
views.case: Paul's language for pagan hostility elsewhere, God gave them over, Romans 1:24-28, describes a comparable dynamic: persistent, self-chosen rebellion eventually meets a divine response that removes any remaining possibility of a change of course, not because God delights in destruction but because Genesis 15:16 already marks Canaan's iniquity as having reached its full measure by this generation, making the hardening here the last stage of judgment on sin that had been building for centuries, not its origin.

debates.bearing: Both views hold that the kings' war making was genuinely their own decision and that God's sovereignty over it served a righteous purpose rather than an arbitrary one; the text itself keeps human responsibility and divine sovereignty side by side without resolving the tension, so that the passage warns readers against presuming they could ever out-hardened their own hearts against a patient God without eventually facing the same outcome.

debates.question: Why does Israel destroy the horses and chariots rather than capture and use them?

views.label: To keep Israel entirely dependent on the LORD rather than on military technology
views.case: God's own instruction is explicit and given before the battle rather than after, hamstring their horses and burn up their chariots, verse 6, a command that forecloses the option of Israel building a chariot corps of its own; Deuteronomy later makes the same principle a standing law for any Israelite king, he must not acquire many horses for himself, Deuteronomy 17:16, suggesting the destruction here was never merely tactical but a deliberate, lasting policy against militarization on Canaanite terms.

views.label: A practical necessity given Israel's lack of chariot infrastructure
views.case: A people that had spent forty years as a wilderness nation without the smiths, wheelwrights, and trained charioteers needed to maintain such equipment could not realistically field captured chariots even if it wished to, so the destruction may reflect what was militarily feasible as much as what was theologically mandated; Israel's later kings, notably Solomon, do eventually acquire horses and chariots at scale, 1 Kings 10:26, suggesting the restriction was tied to this specific moment rather than an absolute principle for every future generation.

debates.bearing: Whichever emphasis is right, the narrative itself credits the destruction directly to God's command and ties it to trust rather than logistics, so that even where practical limits existed, the text wants the reader to see obedience and dependence on the LORD as the operative reason, a reading later Scripture's warnings against trusting chariots and horses consistently reinforces.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond destruction, hardening, and rest already named, several further details deepen the chapter. Jabin, the northern king who initiates the whole coalition, bears a name, or dynastic title, that recurs generations later for another king of Hazor in Judges 4:2, suggesting Jabin functioned less as a single personal name and more as a royal title attached to whoever ruled that city, much as Pharaoh names a throne rather than a man; Hazor's power evidently regenerated more than once before it was finally broken for good.

The verb behind Joshua came upon them suddenly, verse 7, is the same pitom used of the surprise attack at Gibeon in the previous chapter, a repeated narrative signal that speed and surprise, not superior numbers, repeatedly decide these battles; Israel never once wins by matching an enemy's scale, only by striking before that scale can be organized into a defense.

The territory summarized in verses 16 to 17 runs from Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir, as far as Baal-gad, a deliberate south to north sweep meant to bracket the whole land the way a legal deed brackets a property's boundaries. Halak carries the sense of smooth or bare, a fitting name for a stripped, treeless ridge marking the southern edge of the conquest, so that the territorial summary begins and ends at named, physical landmarks rather than vague or approximate borders, reinforcing that this is possession in the fullest sense, not merely a loose sphere of influence.

And the word for eliminate in verse 21, the Anakim, is karat, literally to cut off, the very same verb elsewhere used for cutting a covenant, karat berit, an ironic echo, since covenant cutting normally binds two parties together in solemn relationship while this cutting off severs the Anakim from the land entirely, ending their presence there rather than sealing any relationship to it.

Finally the chapter's last word, shaqat, rest, deliberately differs from the more common noun nuach used elsewhere for settled dwelling; shaqat carries the sense of quiet after storm, the calm that follows a struggle rather than mere absence of activity, which is why the writer of Hebrews can later say plainly that this rest, real as it was, was never the final rest God had in view, since another day and another kind of rest still remained to be spoken of, Hebrews 4:8-9.

typology.type: The destruction of the Anakim, the giants who once broke Israel's nerve
typology.fulfillment: A generation earlier the mere report of these giants had reduced the whole nation to despair, we seemed like grasshoppers in our own sight, Numbers 13:33; here they are simply eliminated, city by city, with no comparable drama attached to their fall. That reversal, an enemy once treated as unconquerable turning out to be entirely within God's reach, anticipates the greater reversal of the gospel, where Christ shares our flesh and blood so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death, Hebrews 2:14-15. The type falls short because a remnant of Anakim still survived in Philistine cities, verse 22, producing Goliath generations later; Christ's victory over the last enemy leaves no remnant of death standing anywhere at all, 1 Corinthians 15:26.

typology.type: Hamstrung horses and burned chariots, a deliberate refusal of worldly military power
typology.fulfillment: Israel is commanded to destroy exactly the technology that made the northern coalition formidable rather than adopt it, so that whatever victories followed could never be credited to captured Canaanite equipment. The same refusal to rely on visible strength runs through the psalmist's confession, some trust in chariots and horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God, Psalm 20:7, and into Paul's description of the church's own warfare, the weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the world, 2 Corinthians 10:4. The type is incomplete because Israel still needed some weapons, swords among them; the greater warfare it foreshadows sets aside worldly weapons altogether in favor of divine power to demolish strongholds.

typology.type: The land at rest from war, the stated goal of the whole conquest
typology.fulfillment: Verse 23 does not end the book's story with more battles promised but with a single settled state, rest, language the book itself later confirms in its own theological summary, the LORD gave them rest on every side, Joshua 21:44. Yet this very rest becomes, in the New Testament's hands, proof that something greater still lay ahead, for if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day, there remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God, Hebrews 4:8-9. The type is real but provisional, since the land's rest was repeatedly disturbed within a generation or two, Judges 3:8, while the rest Christ secures for those who enter it by faith cannot be lost or interrupted again.

typology.type: It was of the LORD to harden their hearts, sovereignty serving righteous judgment
typology.fulfillment: The narrator states plainly that divine hardening, not merely human stubbornness, stood behind the coalition's fatal decision to fight rather than seek terms, echoing the same hardening language used of Pharaoh, Exodus 9:12, and generalized by Paul, God has mercy on whom He wants to have mercy, and He hardens whom He wants to harden, Romans 9:18. This anticipates the sober biblical pattern in which persistent, willful rebellion against clear evidence of God's power, evidence these kings certainly had after Jericho, Ai, and Gibeon, eventually meets a judgment that removes any further opportunity for repentance, a warning the New Testament applies directly to anyone who hardens his heart today while it is still called today, Hebrews 3:15.

study.christ:
Two threads in this chapter run forward to Christ with unusual clarity, and both concern enemies that once seemed too large to face. The first is the Anakim themselves, whose very name had once dissolved a whole generation's courage into despair, we seemed like grasshoppers in our own sight, Numbers 13:33, and who are here simply removed from the land, city by city, without any of the earlier drama their name once carried. What made the difference was never Israel's growth in military capacity between the two generations; it was the difference between believing the report of giants and believing the report of God. Hebrews reads the greater version of this defeat directly onto Christ, who shares our flesh and blood precisely so that through death He might destroy him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death, Hebrews 2:14-15. The enemy that terrifies is not, in the end, the enemy that wins.

The second thread is the rest that closes the chapter, verse 23, then the land had rest from war, the very outcome the whole conquest has been aiming toward since chapter 1. That rest was real, God kept His word to the letter, and yet the writer of Hebrews insists it was never meant to be the last word on the subject: if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later, through David, about another day, today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts, Hebrews 4:7-9, quoting Psalm 95. A rest disturbed again within a couple of generations, Judges 3:8, could not be the rest God ultimately had in view; it could only point toward it. The greater Joshua, sharing His very name in Hebrew, succeeds where the first Joshua's rest eventually failed, bringing His people into a Sabbath rest that no future war can ever again interrupt, because the last enemy standing against that rest, death itself, has already been put under His feet, 1 Corinthians 15:25-26.

Between these two threads sits the refusal to trust chariots and horses, verses 6 and 9, a small detail that nonetheless anticipates the entire logic of the cross, that God's victories are never won by the resources the world considers decisive. The One who defeats the giants and gives the final rest wins both by weakness rather than by force, laid in a grave rather than riding in a chariot, and precisely there proves stronger than every fear His people have ever needed to overcome.
study.god:
This chapter reveals a God whose reassurance never varies with the size of the threat. Facing five kings in chapter 10 and a coalition vast as the sand of the seashore here, Joshua receives the identical word, do not be afraid, verse 6, a repetition that tells the reader God's power was never actually calibrated to the difficulty of what Israel faced; the size of the enemy changes, the sufficiency of God does not. That constancy across escalating chapters is itself a kind of self-revelation, a God for whom no coalition, however vast, requires Him to work any harder than He already had.

He is also sovereign in a way this chapter does not soften for easy comfort. The kings' hardened resolve to fight, verse 20, is attributed directly to Him, and the effect is their total destruction, receiving no mercy, exactly as had been commanded. This is not a God indifferent to how His sovereignty and human choice relate; it is a God who holds both together without apparent strain, ruling over the very stubbornness that seals a nation's judgment while never removing that nation's own responsibility for having chosen war in the first place, a pattern Scripture repeats from Pharaoh onward without ever fully resolving the mystery for the reader.

And He is, by the chapter's last word, a God who finishes what He starts. Shaqat, rest, closes a book that opened with Moses dead and an untested successor commanded to be strong and courageous; every intervening chapter has been building toward this single quiet clause, and the narrator makes sure the reader connects it explicitly to promise rather than achievement, in keeping with all that the LORD had spoken to Moses, verse 23. This is a God who does not merely win battles; He completes covenants, carrying a promise made to Abraham centuries earlier all the way through slavery, wilderness, and war until not one word of it remains unfulfilled, and then, having finished, gives His people rest rather than simply moving them on to the next demand.

crossReferences.note: The LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, the same divine action and the same verb pattern later applied to the northern kings in verse 20, tying Israel's final conquest to the same sovereign hand that first freed the nation from Egypt.

The spies' report of the Anakim, we seemed like grasshoppers in our own sight, had once dissolved Israel's courage into unbelief; their destruction here directly reverses the failure of faith that kept an entire generation out of the land.

Israel's future king is forbidden to acquire many horses for himself, the same principle behind God's command here to hamstring and burn the captured horses and chariots rather than repurpose them for Israel's own military use.

Caleb specifically names the Anakim and their fortified cities when requesting Hebron as his inheritance, showing that this chapter's victory over the giants is what finally allows an old man's decades-deferred faith to be rewarded.

The book's own theological summary of the conquest, not one of all the LORD's good promises had failed, everything was fulfilled, functions almost as a direct commentary on the events narrated in this chapter.

Goliath, a champion from Gath, descends from the very coastal remnant of Anakim left unconquered in verse 22, showing that an enemy driven from most of the land can still resurface generations later to test Israel's faith again.

Some trust in chariots and horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God, a confession that reads almost as a direct commentary on Israel's God-commanded destruction of the northern coalition's chariots and horses.

God has mercy on whom He wants to have mercy, and He hardens whom He wants to harden, Paul's broader theological statement of the same sovereignty this chapter attributes to God over the northern kings' fatal resolve to fight.

Christ shares our flesh and blood so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death and free those enslaved by fear of it, the greater version of Israel's victory over the giants who once terrified them.

If Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day; there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God. The rest that closes Joshua 11 is read here as real but provisional, pointing to a greater rest still to come.

study.oneStory:
By the time Jabin's coalition assembles at the waters of Merom, the promise God first spoke to Abraham, that his offspring would possess this whole land, has been in motion for centuries, through Egypt, through the wilderness, through Jericho, Ai, Gibeon, and the southern campaign, without a single setback strong enough to derail it. This chapter answers the last remaining objection the story could raise, that a big enough enemy, one with horses and chariots and numbers like the sand of the seashore, might finally be the exception. It is not. The very giants whose report once broke an entire generation's nerve are eliminated in the same campaign, closing a wound the book of Numbers left open for forty years and proving that no fear Israel has ever carried into this land was, in the end, justified.

What this chapter completes, the whole book has been building toward since Moses died: the LORD gave them rest on every side, just as He had sworn to their fathers, a rest hard won yet entirely gifted, since not one Israelite sword forced God's hand at any point along the way. That rest becomes the fragile inheritance the rest of the Old Testament will spend centuries losing and regaining, as Judges records how quickly it unravels once a new generation forgets the God who gave it, and as the exile eventually proves how far even a settled people can fall from a promise once fulfilled.

Yet the deepest resolution the chapter offers is not the land itself but what the land was always a picture of. Hebrews reads this very rest as evidence that an even greater rest still waited beyond it, a rest secured not by conquest but by the finished work of Christ, who defeats the last and greatest giant, death, and brings His people into a Sabbath that cannot again be lost to unbelief, war, or exile, because it rests entirely on Him rather than on anything they have done.

quiz.q: What was different about the northern enemy Israel faced?

options.text: It was a huge coalition with horses and chariots, an army as numerous as the sand of the seashore.
options.note: Verses 4 to 5 stress the vast size and military power of the northern alliance.

options.text: It was a small band easily defeated.
options.note: The opposite: it was the largest and best-armed force Israel had yet faced.

options.text: It refused to fight and surrendered at once.
options.note: The coalition gathered specifically to fight Israel at the waters of Merom, not to surrender.

options.text: It was made up entirely of the Gibeonites.
options.note: The Gibeonites had made peace; this was a coalition of northern kings under Jabin of Hazor.

quiz.q: Why did God have Israel hamstring the horses and burn the chariots?

options.text: So Israel would trust in the LORD rather than in military power.
options.note: Destroying the horses and chariots kept Israel from relying on worldly might, as verse 6 and 9 show.

options.text: Because the horses and chariots were diseased.
options.note: There is no mention of disease; the point was to keep Israel from trusting in such power.

options.text: Because Israel could not afford to feed the horses.
options.note: The reason was spiritual, trusting God not chariots, not the cost of feeding horses.

options.text: To sell them to the Gibeonites for profit.
options.note: They were destroyed, not sold; the aim was reliance on God, not profit.

quiz.q: What happened to the Anakim, the giants?

options.text: Joshua drove them out and destroyed them, so none remained in Israel's land except a remnant in a few coastal cities.
options.note: Verses 21 to 22 record the destruction of the giants who had once terrified Israel.

options.text: They defeated Israel and forced a retreat.
options.note: The reverse: the giants who once terrified Israel were themselves destroyed.

options.text: They made a peace treaty with Joshua.
options.note: Only Gibeon made peace; the Anakim were devoted to destruction, not treated with.

options.text: They were left completely untouched.
options.note: They were eliminated from Israel's land, with only a coastal remnant surviving.

quiz.q: How is the completion of the conquest summarized?

options.text: Joshua took the whole land as the LORD had promised Moses, and the land had rest from war.
options.note: Verse 23 sums up the conquest as the fulfillment of God's promise, ending in rest.

options.text: Joshua conquered only part of the land and gave up.
options.note: The summary says he took the entire land in keeping with all the LORD had spoken, not part of it.

options.text: The land remained at war for many more generations under Joshua.
options.note: The chapter ends with the land at rest from war, not ongoing conflict under Joshua.

options.text: Israel abandoned the land and returned east of the Jordan.
options.note: Israel took the land as their inheritance; they did not abandon it.

quiz.q: What does the rest that ends the conquest point toward?

options.text: The greater and lasting rest secured by Christ, of which the land's rest was only a shadow.
options.note: Hebrews 4 reads the land's rest as a foreshadowing of the Sabbath rest in Christ.

options.text: That God's promises finally failed to be fulfilled.
options.note: The opposite: the rest shows God's promise fulfilled; it points beyond itself to a greater rest, not to failure.

options.text: That Israel would never face any struggle again.
options.note: Later struggles came; this rest was real but partial, pointing to the lasting rest in Christ.

options.text: That the land itself is the final goal of salvation.
options.note: The land's rest is a shadow of the greater rest in Christ, not the ultimate goal.

questions: Israel faced its biggest, best-armed enemy yet, and God still said, do not be afraid. What overwhelming situation are you facing where you need to hear that same word from God?
God had Israel destroy the horses and chariots so they would trust Him rather than military power. What worldly source of security are you tempted to trust instead of God?
The giants that once made Israel's heart melt were finally destroyed. What long-standing fear or seemingly unbeatable obstacle do you need to bring to the God for whom no enemy is too great?
The chapter repeats that Joshua left nothing undone of all the LORD commanded. Where is God calling you to complete, wholehearted obedience rather than a partial response?
The land finally had rest from war, a foretaste of the rest Christ gives. Where are you weary and longing for rest, and how does the promise of rest in Christ speak to you today?

translationNotes.note: Devoting them to destruction renders a form of the Hebrew cherem, as the BSB footnote notes; it recurs in verses 12, 20, and 21.
Harden renders a verb the BSB footnote also gives as stiffen or strengthen; the same word describes the hardening of Pharaoh in Exodus.
The foothills render the Shephelah, the western lowlands of Judea, as the BSB footnote notes; the same term appears in verse 16.
